question:
Three A’s, three B’s, and three C’s are placed in the nine spaces so that each row and column contain one of each letter. If A is placed in the upper left corner, how many arrangements are possible?

[Figure 1](figures/2008_AMC_8_Q14_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Because \(A\) is fixed, the first row is either \(ABC\) or \(ACB\). Handle both possibilities by writing the first row as \(A\,X\,Y\), where \(X\) and \(Y\) are \(B\) and \(C\) in either order.

[Figure 1](figures/2008_AMC_8_Q14_question_fig1.svg)

The first entry of the second row must be \(X\) or \(Y\), since its column already contains \(A\).

If it is \(X\), the last entry of that row cannot be \(X\), which is already in the row, or \(Y\), which is above it. Thus the last entry is \(A\), and the middle entry is \(Y\).

If it is \(Y\), the middle entry cannot be \(Y\), which is already in the row, or \(X\), which is above it. Thus the middle entry is \(A\), and the last entry is \(X\).

Each column then forces its missing letter into the bottom row, giving
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
A&X&Y\\
X&Y&A\\
Y&A&X
\end{array}
\qquad
\begin{array}{ccc}
A&X&Y\\
Y&A&X\\
X&Y&A
\end{array}.
\]
Both grids satisfy every row and column restriction. Every valid grid must follow one of these cases, and different choices change either the first row or the first entry of the second row. Therefore nothing is omitted or counted twice. The number of arrangements is \(2\times2=\boxed{4}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
